title: The burden rolls away
hookLine: in Bunyan's story, Christian's burden falls off at the cross and rolls into a tomb

lines: A MAN IN RAGS, BENT OVER.
cards: A heavy backpack does something strange on a long hike. At first you feel every pound. Then you stop noticing, you lean forward without knowing it, and your shoulders forget what light felt like.

Only when you set it down do you realize how bent you'd become. Bunyan's pilgrim starts like that. The first picture of him is a man in rags with a great burden on his back, reading a book and crying out, What shall I do?
He carries that weight through the slough, past the gate, mile after mile. Today, in the story, it finally comes off.

teach.b: Christian runs, with difficulty, up a road fenced with a wall on either side, to a place that rises a little. At the top stands a cross, and below it, a tomb.

Here's how Bunyan tells it: "Just as Christian came up with the Cross, his burden loosed from off his shoulders, and fell from off his back, and began to tumble, and so continued to do, till it came to the mouth of the Sepulchre, where it fell in, and I saw it no more."
Look at what Christian does in that sentence. Nothing. He doesn't untie the straps or throw it off.
He arrives, and the burden loosens. Bunyan, a Protestant preacher, is picturing what he believed about grace: that what Christ did on the cross lifts a weight a person can't lift alone.
The burden falls into the sepulchre, which some readers take as Christ's own tomb, and the narrator never sees it again. Christian stands looking at the cross, amazed, tears running down his cheeks.

Then he says, "He hath given me rest by his sorrow, and life by his death." Rest. That reaches back to Jesus in Matthew's gospel: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."
Christians from different churches describe how that rest comes in different ways: through baptism and the sacraments, through faith, through confession, through a lifetime of being made new.
Bunyan's picture is one man's dream of it.
And the road doesn't end at the cross. Christian keeps walking, lighter now, with a long way still to go.

how: Christians bring their burdens to God in different ways: in personal prayer, in confession or the sacrament of reconciliation, at the communion table, or by laying a written worry at the foot of a cross in some churches.

games.q: you're Christian. you've carried this burden since the City of Destruction. you reach a cross on a little hill. what happens?
o: you work hard to untie it.
it loosens and rolls away by itself.
someone takes it from you and carries it for you.
games.why: it loosens from his shoulders and tumbles into the tomb, and the narrator sees it no more.

practice: Name one weight you've carried so long you've stopped noticing it: a grudge, a worry, a regret. Breathe out and let your shoulders drop, as if the straps had loosened on their own.
If you pray, bring it to the cross, or rest with come unto me; if you don't, let it be set down for now.
